readings.title: The walking map made by residents
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A city walking map usually shows the shortest line between two places. For residents of Hillview, that was not always the most useful information. A steep staircase connected the railway station to the main square, but it was difficult for people pushing shopping carts. Another route was longer yet offered benches and a gentle slope. A neighborhood group decided to produce a map that described these differences instead of recommending one route for everyone.

Volunteers walked each street in pairs. They noted steps, surfaces, crossings, places to rest, and sections without shade. They did not label a path simply easy or difficult, because the same feature could affect walkers differently. A parent with a stroller might avoid steps, while another resident might care more about a safe crossing. The map therefore showed concrete features and allowed users to choose according to their own needs.

During an early trial, the group discovered that printed information became outdated quickly. Construction blocked one crossing for several weeks, and a bench marked on the map was removed. Rather than abandon paper copies, volunteers added a revision date and a telephone number for reporting changes. A version at the community center could be updated more frequently, and staff helped visitors compare it with older copies.

The project attracted attention from the transport department, which used the observations when planning repairs. Still, the group made clear that the map was not a promise that every route would always be open. Conditions could change after a storm or roadworks. Its value lay in providing practical information usually absent from official street plans and in treating local residents as knowledgeable observers. Walking became a question of suitable choices, rather than simply distance.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: A mentor's question notebook
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When Lina became the manager of a small warehouse, she paired each new employee with an experienced colleague. She expected the experienced workers to explain routines and answer questions. Within a month, however, two newcomers made the same labeling mistake. Both said their mentors had been helpful. The problem was that an important exception had seemed so obvious to experienced staff that nobody had mentioned it.

Lina introduced a question notebook beside the training desk. New employees could write down anything they found confusing, without signing their names. Mentors discussed the questions during a short weekly meeting and added useful explanations to the training guide. The notebook was not used to rank newcomers or criticize mentors. Its purpose was to reveal gaps between what experienced workers assumed and what a beginner actually knew.

One question concerned a red sticker used on packages awaiting inspection. A newcomer thought it meant the package should be sent immediately because it looked urgent. The discussion led the team to add a written label as well as color. Another question revealed that instructions described an older screen in the warehouse software. Correcting that page prevented confusion for the next group of employees. Small questions were producing improvements beyond individual training sessions.

After several months, Lina still valued personal mentoring. A document could not notice when someone looked uncertain or demonstrate a difficult movement patiently. But she no longer treated knowledge as something that moved only from expert to beginner. New employees were also helping the warehouse see familiar routines more clearly. The notebook worked because the team responded to questions and changed instructions when necessary. Without that response, it would have become another container for concerns that nobody read.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: A station locker for local food
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
For small farms outside Marston, selling vegetables in town involved a difficult choice. Delivering to individual homes took hours, while a full day at a market kept farmers away from other work. A cooperative tried another arrangement: customers ordered online and collected boxes from cooled lockers near the railway station. Farmers brought all the orders to one location twice a week. Commuters could collect them on their way home.

The first month exposed a weakness in the plan. Some customers worked late, and their collection codes expired before they reached the station. Others could not judge how much food would fit in a standard box. The cooperative extended the collection period and published photographs showing typical contents beside ordinary kitchen objects. It also offered a smaller box. These changes were based on complaints rather than on a large advertising campaign.

The lockers reduced the time farmers spent making separate deliveries, but they introduced new costs. Cooling used electricity, and somebody had to clean the compartments and check that doors closed properly. The cooperative included these expenses when comparing the service with its previous system. Counting only the reduced driving time would have made the savings appear greater than they really were. Customers were told that seasonal availability could change the contents of a box.

After six months, the cooperative kept the lockers but continued a small market stall on Saturdays. Some customers valued speaking directly with growers, and several did not use online ordering. The organizers concluded that convenience had different meanings for different people. A station collection point served many commuters well, but it was one part of a varied sales system. Its success depended on reliable operation and realistic choices, not on replacing every older way of buying food.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: Learning in short sessions
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
After returning to work, Daniel enrolled in an evening language course. He planned to study for three hours every Sunday, but family visits and household tasks often consumed the afternoon. When he missed a session, the next week's material felt even harder. His teacher suggested a different schedule: ten minutes on most weekdays, with a longer session only when time permitted. Daniel was skeptical that such short periods could accomplish anything.

The teacher did not ask him to squeeze an entire lesson into ten minutes. Instead, she helped him choose one small task for each session. On Monday he recalled words from the previous class without looking at his notes. On Tuesday he listened to a brief conversation and wrote its main point. On Wednesday he used several new expressions in a message. The tasks required attention, but their limited size made it easier to begin.

Daniel placed a card beside the kettle to remind himself to study after breakfast. He marked completed sessions on a calendar, though he avoided treating one missed day as a reason to abandon the week. After a month, he could remember more expressions during class discussions. This was encouraging, but the teacher cautioned that short sessions were not a complete substitute for extended practice. Writing a full essay or having a sustained conversation still required longer periods.

The change helped because it matched Daniel's actual routine. Another learner might have a quiet Sunday and prefer a different plan. The teacher's broader advice was to design regular opportunities for active practice and adjust them when circumstances changed. A study schedule was a tool for learning, not a promise that had to be kept perfectly. Small sessions mattered when they formed a useful pattern, not merely because they were short.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

translation.stem: Learning does not stop when people leave school. A new job, a change in technology, or an unfamiliar responsibility may require adults to develop fresh skills. Finding time can be difficult, especially when work and family duties compete for attention. It helps to choose a specific goal and divide it into smaller tasks. Progress may be slow at first, but regular practice makes new knowledge easier to use. Asking questions is also important. A beginner's question can reveal an unclear instruction that experienced people have stopped noticing. When workplaces welcome such questions, they support both individual learning and improvements in everyday practice. Education then becomes part of ordinary life rather than a separate activity reserved for a classroom.
translation.referenceAnswer: 离开学校并不意味着学习停止。新工作、技术变化或陌生职责都可能要求成年人掌握新技能。当工作和家庭责任争夺注意力时，尤其难以抽出时间。选择明确目标并将其分成较小任务会有所帮助。最初进步可能缓慢，但经常练习使新知识更易于运用。提问同样重要。初学者的问题可能揭示老手已经不再注意的不明确说明。工作场所欢迎这类问题时，既支持个人学习，也推动日常实践改进。于是教育成为普通生活的一部分，而非只在教室进行的独立活动。
translation.explanation: 注意 compete for attention 的自然表达，rather than 表示而不是，that 引导定语从句修饰 instruction。

writing.stem: Write an essay entitled A Study Plan I Can Keep. Describe a realistic learning goal, explain how to find regular study time, and discuss how to handle interruptions. Write at least 100 English words.
writing.sampleAnswer:
A useful study plan should fit a person's real life. My current goal is to explain my work clearly in English. Instead of trying to memorize a whole textbook quickly, I plan to learn several useful expressions each week and practice them in short descriptions of familiar tasks.

I can usually find fifteen minutes after breakfast. During that time, I will recall earlier expressions and use them in a new sentence. On a free weekend, I can record a longer explanation and listen for unclear parts. Some days will be interrupted by work or family needs. If that happens, I will continue the next day rather than abandon the plan. Regular practice and sensible adjustments will help me make progress without expecting a perfect timetable.
writing.explanation: 说明具体目标、可用时间、主动练习和中断后的恢复策略，避免空泛地声称每天长时间学习。
